checked.claim: Meta allows cosmetic-procedure ads targeted 18+. Since 22 Jul 2026 health and wellness ads are reviewed on their claims rather than by product category, so before/after images are no longer auto-rejected. Health targeting was removed in 2022 and 2024, detailed-targeting exclusions on 31 Mar 2025, and lower-funnel events were restricted from 2025 (US first).
evidence: transparency.meta.com, facebook.com, run1ads.ai, clikim.com, socialmediatoday.com and tracklution.com were unreachable. GitHub searches for the 22 July 2026 claims-based change found nothing. That change rests only on the researcher's secondary sources and should be re-checked on Meta's own page before anyone relies on before/after creative.

Partial confirmation from Meta's Community Standards (organic content, not ads): under Restricted Goods and Services > Health and Wellness, Meta restricts to adults 18+ any content that attempts to buy, sell, mention or ask for cosmetic procedures, promotes them, or depicts before/after skin transformations that imply negative self-perception. Organic Page, Instagram and creator posts are therefore age-gated too, not only ads. https://github.com/bebetterest/content-rules-corpus/blob/090a22465cc23c94e6deb3151cada709980e43f3/all_rules/platforms/english/meta/meta-community-standards.md (around line 2507)

The 18+ rule for cosmetic-procedure ads and the 2022 removal of sensitive health targeting match background knowledge (high confidence). The Jan 2024 and 31 Mar 2025 targeting changes and the 2025 lower-funnel restriction are plausible but were not checked in this run.

checked.claim: LINE Ads Platform Thailand screening guidelines (version dated 27 May 2020) ban before/after images or videos and claims about medical treatment results.
evidence: lineforbusiness.com, terms.line.me and terms2.line.me were unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED), and no mirror was found on GitHub.
The researcher already flagged the guideline as dated 2020. It must be re-checked against the current LAP Thailand and LINE OA guidelines before any spend. Treat as low-to-medium confidence.

checked.claim: A draft Consumer Protection Act amendment would require paid influencers to disclose ads and brand relationships, including gifted or discounted services, with consultation to 10 Oct 2026. OCPB warned influencers in Oct 2025. Influencers earning 1.8M THB or more a year from online selling or promotion need a direct-marketing licence.
checked.correction: The draft amendment and consultation date are unverified: bakermckenzie.com, silklegal.com, mondaq.com, aseanconsumer.org, nationthailand.com and galalaw.com were all blocked. The 1.8M THB detail is mis-stated. Under the OCPB direct-marketing regime (Direct Sales and Direct Marketing Act), individuals selling goods or services online with annual revenue of no more than 1,800,000 THB are exempt from registering as direct marketers. It is a registration (จดทะเบียน), not a 'licence'. Juristic persons get no exemption and must register from day one whatever their revenue. The threshold is tied to selling through direct-marketing channels, not to paid promotion as such. Whether an influencer who only promotes, without selling, must register is unclear. This matters more for a Thai company that sells Shuriring packages online than for creators.
evidence: Secondary Thai summary of OCPB registration rules: 'บุคคลธรรมดา: มีรายได้จากการขายออนไลน์ไม่เกิน 1,800,000 บาทต่อปี (หากเกินเกณฑ์ ต้องจดทะเบียนภายใน 30 วัน); นิติบุคคล: ไม่มีการยกเว้น'. https://github.com/SatangThevalue/ai-skills/blob/main/skills/finance/thai-business-license-guide/SKILL.md (medium-low confidence; matches background knowledge of a 2021 ministerial exemption)
The draft's coverage of gifted or discounted services, if enacted, would align with TikTok's own definition of branded content, which includes gifted services (verified above).

checked.claim: Consumer ads for medical devices in Thailand need Thai FDA approval under the Medical Device Act. Ads promoting 'Ultraformer III' or claims about what it does could be treated as device ads. How Thailand treats a foreign clinic naming a device brand, and Thai FDA rules on HIFU, were not researched.
evidence: medical.fda.moph.go.th, asiaactual.com and elendilabs.com were unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED).

Background, medium confidence: Thai medical-device advertising approvals are issued with 'ฆพ.' numbers, and approved clinic ads carry 'ฆสพ.' numbers. The advice to use the device name only as a factual label is reasonable.

Market note: Thai clinics already advertise the newer model under a Thai transliteration, 'อัลตร้าฟอร์เมอร์ เอ็มพีที (Ultraformer MPT)', for example a Hat Yai clinic site: https://github.com/chewpichai/kimlineclinic/blob/main/messages/th.json. Device-name keywords are therefore contested by Thai-licensed clinics, which can more easily report foreign ads.

checked.claim: Thailand's PDPA very likely applies to a Korean clinic collecting Thai residents' face photos and health data via LINE. Face photos and health data are sensitive and need explicit consent. Cross-border transfer rules apply, and a Thai representative may be needed. Fines reach several million baht.
checked.correction: Mostly right, checked against the English text of the PDPA B.E. 2562 (Gazette 27 May 2019). Section 5 para 2: the Act applies to controllers outside Thailand that offer goods or services to data subjects in Thailand, whether or not payment is made, or that monitor their behaviour. Section 26: health data and biometric data need explicit consent. One correction: 'biometric data' is defined as data from technical processing of physical or behavioural traits used to identify a person, such as facial-recognition, iris or fingerprint data. A plain face photo is therefore not automatically biometric. Pre-consultation photos become sensitive when they reveal health information (skin condition, treatment) or are processed for recognition. Section 28: transfers abroad need an adequate destination standard or an exception, such as consent after being told the standard is inadequate, contract performance, or legal compliance. Section 29 covers certified group policies and appropriate safeguards. Section 37(5): a s.5 para 2 controller must designate in writing a representative located in Thailand. The s.38 exemption does not apply where s.26 sensitive data is processed. Penalties: administrative fines up to 5M THB for s.26 breaches and s.28 transfers of s.26 data (s.84), and up to 3M THB for s.28, s.37 and similar breaches (s.83). Criminal penalties reach 6 months and/or 500k THB, or 1 year and/or 1M THB where the misuse is for unlawful gain (s.79). Courts can add punitive damages up to 2x actual damages (s.78). Full enforcement from 1 June 2022 is background knowledge (high confidence). Reusing patient photos in marketing needs separate explicit consent, which the researcher correctly noted.
evidence: PDPA English text (Gazette No. 136 Ch. 69 Gor, 27 May 2019): https://github.com/MobileCommerceLab/privacy_law_corpus/blob/main/corpus_documents/plain_text_files/english_text_files/original_english_text_files/Thailand%20(Personal%20Data%20Protection%20Act%202019%20(PDPA)).txt. Sections 5, 26 (including the biometric definition), 28, 29, 37(5), 38, 78, 79, 83 and 84 were extracted and read.
pdpc.or.th was unreachable, so later PDPC cross-border notifications (believed to be the s.28/s.29 rules in force from about 2024) and any adequacy list covering Korea were not checked.

checked.claim: Google Ads' Healthcare & Medicines policy applies worldwide, requires compliance with local law in each targeted location, and bans speculative or experimental treatments (since Oct 2019). Thailand-specific cosmetic rules are unconfirmed. Search ads on Thai keywords are probably the lowest-risk paid channel.
evidence: support.google.com and netpeak.us were unreachable (EGRESS_BLOCKED).

Background, high confidence: Google does require advertisers to follow local law in targeted locations, and it announced a ban on speculative or experimental medical treatment ads (such as unproven stem-cell therapy) in Sept 2019. Background, medium confidence: health conditions are restricted in personalised targeting. The before/after claim is not confirmed.

'Lowest-risk' is an opinion. Search ads targeted to Thailand are still ads for a medical facility shown in Thailand, so the s.38 question and Thai word restrictions still apply. 'Ultraformer' and 'Shurink' are Classys trademarks, and Google's trademark policy can limit their use in ad text if the owner complains (background, medium). Get written authorisation or genuine-device documentation from Classys or its distributor.

checked.claim: The Thai-side legal risk of recruiting Thai patients for Korea falls on local intermediaries: unlicensed medical activity, event organisers and travel packaging, where an outbound tour licence may be needed (inference). Thai authorities warn that complications from surgery abroad cannot be pursued in Thailand. Korea requires foreign-patient attraction registration.
evidence: bangkokpost.com, hfocus.org, portal.info.go.th, greenproksp.com, trade.gov and wongnai.com were unreachable.

Citation inconsistency: the same URL (hfocus.org/content/2024/01/29618) is cited in claim 5 for a DoHSS warning to beauty-clinic doctors and here for a warning about surgery abroad. This claim's summary attributes the warning to 'Thai authorities' while its detail says 'the Medical Council'. One of the two uses may be a mis-citation, so re-open the article before quoting either.

Verified supporting rule: Medical Council ethics clause 22 (B.E. 2565) bars Thai physicians from taking compensation for sending patients. The trade.gov model of Thai clinics acting as agents for Korean hospitals therefore creates ethics exposure for any Thai doctor involved, on top of the intermediary risks listed. https://github.com/narze/ratchagitja.md/blob/main/web/src/content/ratchagitja/ง%20พิเศษ/139/272/17236542.md

Background, medium confidence: the outbound tour business licence under the Tourism Business and Guide Act B.E. 2551 exists and requires a security deposit. Whether a medical-referral agent needs one depends on whether it sells travel or accommodation packages. The researcher correctly labels this an inference.

missed_important_points: Verification limits: every source domain the researcher cited was blocked in this run (EGRESS_BLOCKED/403), and the WebSearch budget was used up. The highest-stakes items rest only on the original researcher's reading of news pages: the April 2026 hotel arrest and sentence, the DoHSS figures and platform meeting of 23 Apr 2026, the Medical Council 2024 details, the 5 Aug 2026 judgment, and Meta's 22 Jul 2026 change. Re-open them before they go into client material.

Penalty type changed: the Medical Facility Act B.E. 2541 is in Schedule 1 of the Act on Fines-as-Pinai B.E. 2565 (Gazette 24 Oct 2022). From about late Oct 2023, its fine-only offences, likely including advertising without approval, are non-criminal 'pinai' fines rather than crimes. Offences that can carry jail are unaffected. Source: https://github.com/DRepresser/Law (data/พระราชบัญญัติว่าด้วยการปรับเป็นพินัย พ.ศ. 2565.txt), ss.39 and 41 and Schedule 1 item 141.

Referral-fee ban for Thai doctors (verified): Medical Council Regulation on Medical Ethics B.E. 2565, clause 22, bars giving or receiving money or benefits for receiving or sending patients. Clause 20 bars hiring or allowing others to advertise a doctor's practice falsely or with exaggeration. Paying a Thai clinic or Thai doctor per referred patient is therefore an ethics violation for them. This hits the 'Thai partner clinic as agent' model directly. Source: https://ratchakitcha.soc.go.th/documents/17236542.pdf (mirror: github.com/narze/ratchagitja.md).

Platform takedown channel (verified): the Royal Decree on Digital Platform Services that Must Be Notified B.E. 2565 (Gazette 23 Dec 2022, in force about Aug 2023) requires platforms serving Thailand to notify ETDA, name an in-Kingdom coordinator if based abroad, and have measures against illegal goods, services and content. This is the mechanism behind DoHSS takedown requests. Expect reported Thai-targeted clinic ads to be removed whatever the advertiser's location.

TikTok is effectively closed for paid creator content (verified): the Branded Content Policy (Apr 2026) prohibits 'any medical institutions, treatments or devices' and 'cosmetic clinics', and a gifted treatment counts as branded content. The Community Guidelines (effective 13 Sep 2025) also make promoting cosmetic surgery, 'including referrals', age-restricted and ineligible for the For You feed. Organic TikTok reach for clinic content is therefore throttled as well, not just paid content. Whether non-surgical HIFU falls under 'cosmetic surgery' is ambiguous.

Meta organic content is age-gated too (verified): the Community Standards restrict to adults 18+ any post that offers, mentions or promotes cosmetic procedures, and before/after skin posts implying negative self-perception. This covers the clinic's own Thai-language Page and Instagram posts and creators' organic posts, not only ads.

PDPA details the researcher left open (verified from the Act text): a representative in Thailand is mandatory under s.37(5) for a s.5 para 2 foreign controller, and the s.38 exemption is unavailable when health data (s.26) is processed. Plain face photos are not 'biometric data' by definition, but treatment photos usually count as health data. Fines go up to 5M THB (s.84), criminal liability up to 1 year or 1M THB (s.79), and punitive damages up to 2x (s.78). Budget for a Thai representative and a Thai-language privacy notice and consent flow in the LINE OA before collecting photos.

'Only' and '원툴' wording risk: a 2026 Thai clinic-marketing source lists 'เท่านั้น' ('only/exclusively') among DoHSS-flagged ad words, next to 'อันดับ 1', 'ที่สุด' and 'รับประกันผลลัพธ์'. A literal Thai rendering of 'Shurink one-tool master / only Shurink' ('เฉพาะ...เท่านั้น', 'ผู้เชี่ยวชาญ') is likely to be flagged. Consider factual framing such as 'a clinic that performs Ultraformer/Shurink treatments' instead. Low-medium confidence; source https://github.com/champ197/master

Thai clinic-advertising criteria reportedly also bar before/after comparisons, patient or celebrity testimonials, and discount, gift or lucky-draw promotions ('ลด แลก แจก แถม'). The researcher covered this only through LINE's policy. Thai price promotions ('Thai patient discount', 'free RF with HIFU') in Thai-targeted ads carry DoHSS risk. Low-medium confidence (background); check against the current MoPH/DoHSS advertising criteria.

Online pre-consultation grey zone: Thai law defines medical practice to include examination and diagnosis. A Korea-licensed doctor giving LINE video 'assessments' to people physically in Thailand may be argued to be unlicensed practice in Thailand, the same logic as the hotel case. Keep LINE contact to general information and quotes, and hold the examination and diagnosis in Korea. Low-medium confidence; ask Thai counsel.

Korean-side constraints on paying Thai intermediaries (background, medium confidence; outside the Thai-law angle but decisive): Korea's Medical Service Act art. 27(3) bans inducing or brokering patients for money, with an exception only for registered foreign-patient attraction under the Medical Overseas Expansion Act. The clinic should be registered as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관, and paid agents and affiliate influencers should be registered 유치업자. Per-patient commissions to unregistered Thai creators could break Korean law.

Tax-refund messaging (medium-low confidence, verify): Korea's VAT refund for foreign patients' cosmetic procedures was reportedly allowed to lapse at the end of 2025. Thai ads promising a 'tax refund' could now be misleading under both Thai consumer rules and Korean ad rules.

Trademark and genuine-device issue: 'Ultraformer', 'Ultraformer MPT' and 'Shurink' are Classys marks, and Thai-licensed clinics already bid on the Thai transliteration 'อัลตร้าฟอร์เมอร์'. Using the marks in ad text, especially on Google, can be restricted after a trademark complaint. Obtain Classys genuine-device or authorised-user documentation, which also answers Thai consumers' fake-HIFU worries.

research.angle: Concrete marketing channels and tactics for a Korean Shurink-only clinic (슈리링의원, "슈링크 원툴 장인") to reach Thai customers: platforms (Gangnam Unni/UNNI, LINE OA, TikTok/Facebook/Lemon8/Pantip), Thai price anchors and keywords, influencers, government programs, entry-friction and compliance caveats. NOTE ON METHOD: WebFetch was blocked by the egress proxy for every domain tried (mohw.go.kr, asiae, koreatimes, lycorp, linenewsroom, cresclab, startuprecipe, koreahealthtour) and the session's WebSearch budget ran out partway through. So the findings rest on search-result summaries I could not open and read in full. Anything drawn only from background knowledge has no URL and is marked low confidence.

findings.claim: Thailand is a fast-growing source market for Korean aesthetic medicine. In 2025 Korea had about 58,000 Thai foreign patients (+52.3% YoY, 5th among countries). Thai dermatology visits rose 62.0% and plastic-surgery visits 140.9%. Total foreign patients passed 2 million in 2025.
findings.detail: The numbers come from the MOHW press release '2025년 외국인 환자 유치 200만 돌파' (published around 2026-04-24, re-posted by KHIDI's koreahealthtour.co.kr and Medifonews). I saw them only in search summaries because fetching the pages was blocked. For context, 2024 had 1.17M foreign patients, with dermatology at 56.6% (705k). The same summary says the government is running country-specific marketing in 12 countries including Thailand, using foreign influencers and fam tours for travel agencies. What this means for the clinic: the Thai segment is growing fast and dermatology/lifting is its core demand. It is still much smaller than China or Japan, so there is room for a niche 'lifting specialist' to become known.

findings.claim: Gangnam Unni (강남언니, Healing Paper) is now the main cross-border booking platform for Thai users. Its Thai-language 'UNNI' app launched in November 2024, and within 7 months Thai users booking Korean clinics grew tenfold. Skin lifting is a top interest.
findings.detail: Reported in June 2025 (Asiae, Digital Daily, MoneyS, Platum, Edaily). The app reached #2 in Beauty on Google Play Thailand and #11 in Health & Fitness on the iOS App Store. Its core users are women in their late 20s to early 30s. They are most interested in skin lifting, rhinoplasty and fat procedures. The app offers Thai-language price comparison, auto-translated reviews, consultation and booking. A Korea Times headline from April 2026 says foreign users passed 700,000 (headline only; article not read). This is the most direct pay-to-be-found channel for a Shurink-only clinic, because 'lifting' is exactly what these users search for.

findings.claim: Gangnam Unni's concierge service 'Unnie Guide' (launched March 2026) handles clinic booking and interpretation through LINE, WhatsApp and WeChat. As of 12 Aug 2026, Thailand was the #1 nationality among its users.
findings.detail: By 12 Aug 2026 it had received more than 1,600 requests from 73 countries, growing about 30% a month. The top five countries were Thailand, Taiwan, the US, China and Australia. This shows two things: (a) Thai demand for Korean aesthetic procedures is currently the strongest of any foreign group on the leading platform, and (b) LINE is the chat channel Thai patients expect. The clinic should ask to be included in Unnie Guide's partner network as well as the UNNI listing. Fee and commission terms are not public, so they need to be asked for. Separately, an Aju Press story dated 2026-09-08 describes a data breach that exposed people's cosmetic-procedure choices. I could not see which company was involved. Check before sharing Thai patient data with any platform.

findings.claim: LINE is Thailand's default messaging and brand channel, with about 54-56M Thai users. A Thai-language LINE Official Account should be the clinic's main hub for inquiries, booking and follow-up.
findings.detail: Secondary sources (Hashmeta, Fortune Thailand, Audience-IQ, LY Corp) cite 54M+ MAU (roughly 75-80% of the population), 92%+ weekly use among internet users, and more than 70% following at least one business account. One claim that '85% of Thai shoppers interact with a brand on LINE OA before visiting a website' comes from a marketing blog; treat it as indicative only. Thai government agencies, including the Ministry of Public Health, run LINE OAs, so Thais are used to doing healthcare admin on LINE. LY Corp also announced 'LINE HEALTH' at LINE Conference Thailand 2025 (details not read). Useful features: rich menu (price / book / reviews / doctor / location / Thai coordinator chat), auto-reply plus a manual chat handover, broadcast with audience tags, and coupons.

findings.claim: LINE OA Thailand pricing (2025-2026, per Thai vendor blogs): Free plan with 300 broadcast messages a month; Basic at 1,280 THB/month for 15,000 messages; Pro at 1,780 THB/month for 35,000 messages. The MyCustomer CRM add-on costs 369 THB/month on Free and Basic and is included in Pro.
findings.detail: Search summaries of Cresclab (2026 update), Sellsuki, deemarketingth and NIPA; the plan structure changed on 1 Aug 2024 (EX10). One summary gives the Basic overage as 0.10 THB per message; Pro overage was not confirmed. Only broadcast/push messages count against the quota, so 1:1 chat replies are not limited. For a single clinic starting out, Free or Basic is enough. Two things to confirm on lineforbusiness.com/th: current prices, and whether a Korea-registered business can open or verify a Thailand-region OA (the region affects pricing, verified badge and ads).

findings.claim: Thai clinics sell Ultraformer III heavily and cheaply at home, so the Korean clinic is competing against a strong domestic price anchor. Examples: TALISA Clinic from 9,990 THB for 400 shots; Summer Clinic Phuket at 20,500 THB for 800 lines (full face, double chin and neck, with free add-ons); V Square Clinic runs SEO pages such as 'Ultraformer III ราคาโปรโมชัน 2026'.
findings.detail: The Thai market treats Ultraformer as a promotion-driven, price-per-shot product. Chains like V Square own Thai Google results for 'Ultraformer III ราคา' (price) and 'Ultraformer MPT ราคา'. To win, the Korean clinic needs a reason for Thais to do it in Korea rather than at home. Options: (1) 'the original Korean Shurink, done by a doctor who only does Shurink'; (2) transparent shot counts and proof of genuine cartridges (a common Thai worry about fake or refilled tips); (3) a total Korean price that is clearly competitive when bundled with a trip. Get the clinic's own KRW price before making any 'cheaper than Thailand' claim. Thai promotion prices change often.

findings.claim: Thai consumers know the device as 'Ultraformer III' or 'Ultraformer MPT', not 'Shurink'. All Thai-facing content and SEO should connect the two names, for example 'Shurink = Ultraformer III ต้นตำรับเกาหลี' (the Korean original).
findings.detail: Thai clinic pages use the brand names 'Ultraformer III' and 'Ultraformer MPT' with Thai benefit wording such as 'ยกกระชับ ปรับรูปหน้าเรียว' (lift, firm, slim the face) and 'ยกหน้า' (face lift), and they emphasise ราคา / โปรโมชัน (price / promotion). Suggested Thai keyword set, to check in Google Keyword Planner and TikTok search (not volume-checked): 'Ultraformer III เกาหลี', 'Ultraformer เกาหลี ราคา', 'ทำ Ultraformer ที่เกาหลี', 'HIFU เกาหลี', 'คลินิกเกาหลี', 'ยกกระชับหน้า เกาหลี', and 'Shurink' itself. Have a native Thai speaker check the transliteration 'อัลตร้าฟอร์เมอร์'; most Thai pages seem to keep the English brand name. In Korea, 'Shurink Universe' (슈링크 유니버스) is the domestic name for Ultraformer MPT, so the clinic should say clearly which machine and generation it uses.

findings.claim: Facebook, TikTok and LINE are the three core commerce and social channels in Thailand. Thai clinics already turn short-form TikTok content into inquiries.
findings.detail: A ResearchAndMarkets report (May 2025) names Facebook, Instagram, LINE Shopping, X and TikTok as the dominant social-commerce platforms. The market was USD 4.38B in 2024, forecast at 10.2% CAGR to about USD 8.46B by 2030, and influencer-led live selling is common. A Thai agency blog (oho.chat) cites a Thai eye clinic that reached 79.4K TikTok followers and 600K+ views with review and education content, which produced inquiries. TikTok discover pages for 'Korean Ultraformer MPT review', 'Vs Line Clinic Seoul Review' and 'All Line Clinic Korea Review' show that foreign visitors already search TikTok for Korean clinic reviews. Suggested approach: TikTok and Reels (with Thai subtitles) showing the procedure first-person, shot counting, the doctor's technique, immediate before/after lighting-controlled footage (only if legally allowed; see compliance finding), and a Facebook Page as the trust layer (reviews, Thai Q&A, Messenger to LINE).

findings.claim: For Thai influencer marketing, micro and macro creators with real engagement convert better than mega influencers, and fake-follower accounts are a known problem in Thailand.
findings.detail: A Korean agency guide to Thai influencers (AJ Marketing, 2026) warns about hiring on follower count alone because of fake accounts and brand-damage cases. It says micro and macro creators with high engagement deliver better purchase conversion than mega influencers. MOHW's own programme also uses foreign influencer fam tours. I did not find verified THB rate cards for Thai KOLs/KOCs, so get quotes rather than rely on rumoured rates. Low-cost option: seed Thai creators who are already in Seoul (Thai students, residents, travellers) with a disclosed sponsored treatment in exchange for content. Korean medical-advertising law restricts testimonial-style ads (see compliance finding), so paid reviews need legal review first.

findings.claim: Pantip and Lemon8 are important for Thai 'research before buying'. Pantip hosts long-form beauty and travel reviews (the 'โต๊ะเครื่องแป้ง' beauty room and 'บลูแพลนเน็ต' travel room), and Lemon8 (ByteDance) is widely used in Thailand for beauty and lifestyle posts.
findings.detail: From background knowledge only; I could not retrieve a source in this session. Suggested tactic: watch Pantip for 'Ultraformer เกาหลี' and 'ทำหน้าที่เกาหลี' threads and answer transparently under an identified clinic account. Do not post disguised reviews: Pantip users and moderators punish covert promotion, and fake reviews would also create legal risk. Post Thai-language carousel explainers on Lemon8 (price breakdown, recovery, how to verify genuine tips).

findings.claim: Korean compliance limits some of these tactics. Soliciting foreign patients generally requires registering as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 (registered foreign-patient provider) under the 의료해외진출법, and working only with registered agencies (유치업자). Medical ads, including SNS and influencer content, are regulated by Medical Service Act Art. 56-57 (for example, restrictions on patient-experience testimonials and prior review for certain media).
findings.detail: From background knowledge; I could not retrieve primary text. I believe there is a commission cap for agency fees, possibly 30% for clinic-level (의원급) providers, and a special rule allowing foreign-language medical ads in places such as international airports and tourist zones. I am not sure of either. Verify with KHIDI or a lawyer before signing agency or platform contracts or running influencer 'review' campaigns. The Thai side (Thai sanatorium advertising rules, Thai PDPA when collecting Thai leads) was not verified.

findings.claim: Entry friction is a real conversion risk for Thai travellers to Korea. Entry refusals in 2023-2024 set off a Thai social-media backlash (a 'แบนเที่ยวเกาหลี' / ban-Korea-travel hashtag) and dented Thai travel sentiment. Whether Thai visitors need K-ETA should be checked at the time of travel.
findings.detail: From background knowledge; I could not retrieve a source. Practical tactic: after a booking, send the patient a Thai/English appointment confirmation on clinic letterhead with the clinic's registration details, so they can show it at immigration. Also put pre-travel K-ETA/entry guidance in the LINE rich menu. This lowers no-shows and builds trust.

recommendations: Step 0, compliance first: confirm or complete registration as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관, and get legal sign-off on Thai-language ads, influencer seeding and before/after content under Medical Service Act Art. 56-57 before spending money. Contract only with registered 유치업자.

Brand bridge: every Thai-facing asset should say 'Shurink (슈링크) = Ultraformer III ต้นตำรับเกาหลี' and state exactly which device generation is used (Ultraformer III vs MPT / Shurink Universe). Frame the 'one-tool master' story in Thai as 'a doctor who does only Ultraformer', with a case count, video of the doctor's own technique, and on-camera proof of genuine cartridges and shot counts.

Platform first, owned channels second: list the clinic on Gangnam Unni's Thai 'UNNI' app and apply to the 'Unnie Guide' concierge network, since Thailand is its #1 nationality and lifting is a top interest. At the same time, check Creatrip, Klook and KKday listings (partner terms unverified).

Open a Thai-language LINE OA, starting on Free or Basic (about 1,280 THB/month per Thai vendor blogs; verify on lineforbusiness.com/th). Build a rich menu with Price (THB and KRW) / Book / Real reviews / Doctor / Map & how to get there / Chat with Thai coordinator / Before your trip (K-ETA, confirmation letter). Tag leads by source (UNNI, TikTok, influencer code) so you can see which channel converts.

Hire or contract a native Thai coordinator (part-time is fine to start) to answer LINE within Thai business hours. Thailand is UTC+7, two hours behind Korea. Fast replies in Thai on LINE are the main conversion lever.

Build a Thai landing page and SEO pages around price-comparison searches ('Ultraformer III เกาหลี ราคา', 'ทำ Ultraformer ที่เกาหลี', 'HIFU เกาหลี'). Include an honest comparison table against typical Thai promotion prices (e.g., TALISA 400 shots at 9,990 THB), but only after the clinic's own KRW prices and the Korean legality of price or discount advertising are confirmed.

Content engine: 3-5 Thai-subtitled short videos a week for TikTok, Reels and Lemon8 (procedure first-person, shot counting, doctor explaining the vector technique, what to expect, downtime). Use the Facebook Page for trust (Thai FAQ, Messenger routed to LINE). Monitor Pantip threads and reply openly as the clinic; never post disguised reviews.

Influencers: start with 5-10 vetted Thai micro creators or KOCs who are already in Seoul (check engagement rates and look for fake-follower patterns). Offer disclosed sponsored treatments, give each a trackable LINE coupon code, and scale only the creators who produce LINE bookings.

Government channels: contact KHIDI and KTO (Bangkok office) about joining their 2026 Thailand programmes (influencer and agency fam tours, roadshows, travel fairs such as the Thai International Travel Fair) rather than exhibiting alone at first.

Remove friction for Thai patients: take international cards and quote in THB. Check whether Alipay+ can take Thai e-wallets such as TrueMoney and whether Thai multi-currency travel cards work at the clinic. Send a bilingual booking-confirmation letter to support entry at immigration.

checked.claim: Thailand is a fast-growing source market: in 2025 Korea had about 58,000 Thai foreign patients (+52.3% YoY, 5th); Thai dermatology visits +62.0%, plastic surgery +140.9%; total foreign patients passed 2 million in 2025; the government runs country-specific marketing in 12 countries including Thailand.
checked.correction: I could not open any primary source, so these 2025 figures are still unconfirmed. The numbers are consistent with each other and with the 2024 baseline I know. 2024 had about 1.17M foreign patients, dermatology was 56.6% (about 705k), and Thailand was about 38k and ranked 5th after Japan, China, the US and Taiwan. 58,000 / 1.523 gives about 38.1k, which matches that baseline. The +140.9% plastic-surgery growth starts from a small base, so it should not be presented as a big absolute number. The statistics count only patients reported by REGISTERED foreign-patient providers (유치의료기관). An unregistered clinic's Thai patients are neither counted nor legally solicitable. Confidence stays medium. Before quoting the numbers to a client, read the actual MOHW release, which normally comes out in April for the previous year.
evidence: WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) and WebFetch returned EGRESS_BLOCKED for mohw.go.kr, koreahealthtour.co.kr, medifonews.com, news.nate.com and korea.net, so none of the cited pages could be opened.

Background knowledge (training to mid-2026): the MOHW 2024 release put foreign patients at about 1.17M, with dermatology at 56.6% and Thailand about 38k in 5th place. This matches the claimed 2025 figure and growth rate. The 2025 release itself was not seen.

checked.claim: LINE is Thailand's default messaging and brand channel with about 54-56M Thai users; a Thai-language LINE Official Account should be the clinic's main hub.
checked.correction: The core claim holds. LINE Thailand's own long-standing figure is about 54M users; '56M' shows up in some later secondary sources. Whether that is 75% or 80% of the population depends on the base (about 66M Thai nationals vs about 72M total population). Drop the '85% of shoppers interact on LINE OA' statistic or label it unsupported. The 'LINE HEALTH' announcement was not verified and should not be relied on. Thai public-health services do run on LINE OA (for example MOPH's 'หมอพร้อม' / Mor Prom), which supports the point that Thais are used to handling healthcare admin on LINE. Using LINE OA as the inquiry, booking and aftercare hub is sound. The limits are in the pricing claim below: region, verification badge and ads eligibility for a Korea-based business.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for lycorp.co.jp, meltwater.com, lineforbusiness.com; no live re-check possible.
Background knowledge: '54 million LINE users in Thailand' is LINE Thailand's widely repeated figure (2022-2025); Mor Prom operated as a LINE OA during and after COVID-19.

checked.claim: LINE OA Thailand pricing: Free 300 messages; Basic 1,280 THB/15,000 messages; Pro 1,780 THB/35,000 messages; MyCustomer add-on 369 THB/month on Free/Basic, included in Pro.
checked.correction: The tiers (Free 300 / Basic 1,280 THB with 15,000 messages / Pro 1,780 THB with 35,000 messages) match what I remember of Thailand's LINE OA structure. I could not confirm current 2026 prices, overage rates or MyCustomer pricing. Thai LINE OA prices are usually quoted EXCLUDING 7% VAT, so add VAT when budgeting. The bigger practical risk is not price but eligibility. A verified account (blue badge) in the Thailand region, premium ID options and LINE Ads Platform access normally require Thai business documentation. A Korea-registered clinic may be limited to an unverified (gray badge) account with no Thai LINE Ads. Confirm on lineforbusiness.com/th or with a Thai LINE agency before committing. Treat confidence as low-medium.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for blog.cresclab.com, sellsuki.co.th, ex10.tech, lineforbusiness.com; no source opened.
Background knowledge only for the tier structure and the gray/blue/green badge system; nothing about 2026 prices is confirmed.

checked.claim: Thai clinics sell Ultraformer III heavily and cheaply at home (TALISA from 9,990 THB/400 shots; Summer Clinic Phuket 20,500 THB/800 lines; V Square SEO pages 'Ultraformer III ราคาโปรโมชัน 2026').
checked.correction: The general point is consistent with what I know: Thai clinics and chains such as V Square sell Ultraformer III and MPT widely, on promotions and priced per shot or per line. The specific prices could not be opened, so the researcher's 'high' confidence should drop to medium. Promotions change monthly, and 'lines' and 'shots' are not comparable units across clinics. Thai clinics ALREADY market the device as 'Korean' (เกาหลี / original Korean), so 'the original Korean Shurink' alone is weak differentiation. The difference has to be the doctor, verified genuine cartridges, a transparent shot count, and a bundled trip experience. Any 'cheaper than Thailand' claim must use the clinic's own all-in THB price. It must also account for the likely end of the Korean VAT refund for foreign tourists' cosmetic procedures from 2026 (see missed points), and it may run into Korean restrictions on comparative ads.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for talisaclinic.com, summerclinicphuket.com and vsquareclinic.co; price points not re-checked.
Background knowledge: Thai clinic marketing commonly uses 'Ultraformer III/MPT ราคา/โปรโมชัน' and 'Korean-original' wording.

checked.claim: Thai consumers know the device as 'Ultraformer III' / 'Ultraformer MPT', not 'Shurink'; Thai content should connect the two names. 'Shurink Universe' is the Korean name for Ultraformer MPT.
checked.correction: This matches my knowledge. Classys sells Shurink in Korea and Ultraformer III abroad; Shurink Universe in Korea is Ultraformer MPT abroad. Thai pages mostly keep the English brand name and use 'ไฮฟู' for HIFU. Don't confuse 'อัลเทอร่า' with Ultraformer: it is the Thai spelling of Ulthera (Merz), the premium HIFU competitor and a useful comparison keyword. Search volume for 'Shurink' in Thailand is probably low, so lead with 'Ultraformer' and use 'Shurink' as the Korean-original story. The Thai keywords still need volume checks. Classys owns the 'Shurink' and 'Ultraformer' trademarks, so check with Classys or a lawyer before building clinic branding and ads around them.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for vsqclinic.com and chiangmaiwellnessclinic.com.
Background knowledge of Classys naming (Shurink / Ultraformer III; Shurink Universe / Ultraformer MPT) and of Thai usage of 'อัลเทอร่า' for Ulthera.

checked.claim: Facebook, TikTok and LINE are the three core commerce/social channels in Thailand (ResearchAndMarkets: USD 4.38B social commerce 2024, 10.2% CAGR to ~USD 8.46B by 2030); Thai clinics convert TikTok content into inquiries; TikTok discover pages show foreigners search for Korean clinic reviews.
checked.correction: Facebook, LINE and TikTok are major channels, but calling them 'the three core' leaves out YouTube, which is among Thailand's largest platforms by reach and fits long-form procedure explainers and vlogs. It also leaves out Instagram, which is smaller but important for Bangkok beauty audiences. The ResearchAndMarkets figures measure social COMMERCE (product selling), not medical-service or travel decisions, and I could not verify them. TikTok 'discover' pages are auto-generated SEO pages and do not show search volume. The biggest missing point is that PAID ads on these platforms face cosmetic-procedure rules. Meta requires 18+ targeting and bars before/after images for cosmetic procedures. TikTok restricts cosmetic-procedure ads. So the before/after footage idea is mostly unusable in paid ads and may also breach Korean medical-ad rules in organic posts.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for businesswire.com, meltwater.com; WebSearch budget exhausted.

Background knowledge: DataReportal-type data consistently ranks Facebook, YouTube, LINE and TikTok as Thailand's top platforms; Meta's 'Personal Health and Appearance' ad policy restricts before/after imagery for cosmetic procedures.

checked.claim: Micro/macro Thai creators with real engagement convert better than mega influencers; fake-follower accounts are a known problem in Thailand.
checked.correction: This is standard industry advice and plausible, but I could not open the AJ Marketing source, and there are no verified THB rate cards. Two legal points need adding. (1) In Korea, a paid or sponsored creator post about the clinic's treatment is treated as the clinic's medical ad. Patient treatment-experience testimonials are restricted under Medical Service Act Art. 56(2), so 'review' content needs legal review. Paid posts also need clear sponsorship disclosure (Korean FTC endorsement guidelines; Thai platforms require paid-partnership labels). (2) Giving free or discounted treatment to foreign creators counts as patient inducement. It is only lawful if the clinic is a registered foreign-patient provider (의료법 Art. 27(3) exception).
evidence: No source could be opened (WebFetch blocked for ajmarketing.io and mohw.go.kr).
Background knowledge of Medical Service Act Art. 27(3) and 56(2); low-medium confidence on exact sub-paragraph numbers.

checked.claim: Pantip and Lemon8 matter for Thai pre-purchase research: Pantip rooms 'โต๊ะเครื่องแป้ง' (beauty) and 'บลูแพลนเน็ต' (travel); Lemon8 is popular for beauty/lifestyle in Thailand.
checked.correction: This matches my knowledge. Pantip is Thailand's largest forum; โต๊ะเครื่องแป้ง is the beauty room and บลูแพลนเน็ต the travel room. Thailand and Japan were Lemon8's early core markets, and it is strongly beauty-focused. Pantip bans covert or undeclared advertising (โฆษณาแฝง), so an identified clinic account with transparent answers is the right approach. The researcher also left out Facebook Groups, such as large Thai 'เที่ยวเกาหลี' (Korea travel) and Korean-beauty groups, which are major pre-trip research venues. Confidence is medium because it rests on my knowledge; no live re-check was possible.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for pantip.com.
Background knowledge of Pantip room names and Lemon8's launch markets.

checked.claim: Korean compliance: soliciting foreign patients requires registration as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 under the 의료해외진출법, and using only registered agencies; medical ads including SNS/influencer content are regulated by Medical Service Act Art. 56-57; possible 30% fee cap for clinics; foreign-language ad exception at airports/tourist zones.
checked.correction: The direction is right; here are the specifics as I know them (medium-low confidence, verify with KHIDI or a lawyer). Registration is under 의료해외진출법 Art. 6. A clinic must have at least one specialist (전문의) in the relevant field and medical-malpractice liability insurance. Registration is time-limited (I believe about 3 years) and needs renewal, and annual reports on foreign-patient numbers are required. Unregistered solicitation, including discounts or brokerage, breaches the Medical Service Act Art. 27(3) ban on patient inducement; the foreign-patient exception applies only to registered providers and agencies. As I recall, the MOHW cap on agency commissions is 15% for tertiary hospitals, 20% for general hospitals and 30% for hospitals and clinics (의원급). The foreign-language ad exception (international airports, ports and similar places) is, I believe, in 의료해외진출법 Art. 15. Art. 56 lists banned ad content: testimonials, superlative or comparative claims, and misleading discount ads. Art. 57 requires prior review for designated media, including large internet and SNS platforms. The brand claims '원툴 장인', 'No.1', 'only' and 'specialist/전문' all need review under Art. 56. Thai side: Thai sanatorium ads need approval under the Sanatorium Act B.E. 2541 and carry a 'ฆพ.' licence number. That rule targets Thai facilities, but Thai platforms may still ask for it. Thailand's PDPA B.E. 2562 (fully in force since 1 June 2022) applies extraterritorially to controllers offering services to people in Thailand (s.5). Health data is sensitive data needing explicit consent (s.26), which matters for LINE lead forms and photo collection.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for law.go.kr; no statute text opened.

Background knowledge of 의료해외진출법 (Arts. 6, 15), 의료법 (Arts. 27(3), 56, 57), Thai Sanatorium Act ad licensing (ฆพ. numbers in Thai clinic ads) and Thai PDPA ss.5/26; article numbers and the 15/20/30% caps are medium-low confidence.

checked.claim: Entry friction is a real conversion risk: 2023-2024 entry refusals triggered the Thai 'แบนเที่ยวเกาหลี' hashtag and hurt Thai travel sentiment; whether Thai visitors need K-ETA should be checked at travel time.
checked.correction: The backlash was real. #แบนเที่ยวเกาหลี trended mainly in 2023 (peaking around Oct-Nov 2023) after viral posts about K-ETA rejections and entry denials. Thai arrivals to Korea then lagged other markets in 2024. The researcher left the K-ETA question open, but it can be stated plainly: Thailand was NOT among the countries temporarily exempted from K-ETA (the exemption covered about 22 countries from April 2023 and was extended at least through end-2025). As far as I know, Thai visitors need an approved K-ETA under the 90-day visa waiver. Check k-eta.go.kr for 2026 changes. The root cause is Korea's large undocumented Thai worker population ('ผีน้อย'). A clinic appointment letter helps, but it does not guarantee entry and only carries weight if issued by a registered provider. The clinic should also avoid anything that could look like facilitating entry for non-medical purposes.
evidence: WebFetch blocked for k-eta.go.kr and en.wikipedia.org; WebSearch budget exhausted.
Background knowledge of the K-ETA temporary exemption list (Thailand excluded), the 2023 Thai social-media backlash, and the 'phi noi' context; medium confidence.

missed_important_points: Verification limit: in this session WebSearch was exhausted (200/200) and every WebFetch domain returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, including the MOHW, KHIDI, LINE, Thai clinics, law.go.kr and K-ETA sites. All verdicts rest on background knowledge up to mid-2026 plus consistency checks. Re-check the high-stakes numbers (2025 MOHW statistics, LINE OA prices, Thai clinic prices, fee caps and article numbers) with live access before giving them to the client.

The VAT refund for foreign tourists' cosmetic procedures (조세특례제한법 Art. 107-3 special refund) was set to end on 31 Dec 2025. The 2025 tax-revision plan proposed not extending it. If it ended, Thai patients no longer get roughly 7-8% back from 2026, which weakens the 'cheaper in Korea' pitch. Medium-low confidence; verify the current status.

Paid-ads feasibility is the main channel constraint. Meta requires 18+ targeting and bans before/after images for cosmetic procedures. TikTok restricts cosmetic-procedure ads. LINE Ads and the verified badge in Thailand usually require Thai business or licensing documents, and Thai clinic ads carry a Thai 'ฆพ.' ad-approval number that a Korean clinic cannot get. Plan on organic content, creators, LINE OA, SEO/Google and partnerships more than on paid social ads.

Target Thais who are already planning a trip to Korea rather than persuading them to fly just for Shurink. Channels that carry travel intent include Pantip บลูแพลนเน็ต, Facebook Korea-travel groups, OTAs and experience platforms (for example Klook, KKday, Trip.com and Creatrip-type foreigner booking sites), and Thai travel agencies. Time campaigns to Thai peak travel to Korea (autumn foliage, winter, and holiday periods such as Songkran and New Year). Timing points are low-medium confidence.

Thais in Korea use Google Maps and Google reviews rather than Naver. A Google Business Profile with Thai/English information, verified reviews and THB-equivalent pricing is a cheap, high-intent channel.

Registration as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 is a prerequisite, not just a compliance box. It is what makes discounts, agency partnerships and foreign-language ads lawful, and it gives access to KHIDI/Medical Korea programmes (country roadshows, fam tours, Thai-market promotions) that the researcher mentioned only as government activity.

The brand message '슈링크 원툴 장인' needs review under Korean medical-ad rules on superlatives, comparisons and 'specialist/전문' wording, and under Classys trademark rules for 'Shurink/Ultraformer'. The same care applies to Thai-language versions ('the best', 'the only', 'No.1').

Thai PDPA (health data is sensitive and needs explicit consent; the law applies to foreign clinics serving people in Thailand) must be built into LINE OA lead forms, photo consultations and CRM tagging. Korean PIPA also applies once the data is stored in Korea.

Trust signals specific to Thai buyers should be operational, not just messaging: show cartridge authenticity and the shot counter on camera, quote an all-in price in THB up front (Korean clinics' 'foreigner pricing' has been criticised in the press), provide a Thai-speaking coordinator or interpreter, and handle aftercare over LINE after the patient flies home.

Thai-friendly payment and booking deposits (cards, and wallets that work in Korea through networks such as Alipay+, possibly including TrueMoney; low confidence) lower the chance of no-shows. Check this with the clinic's payment provider.

research.angle: Thai-to-Korea travel and medical tourism context, 2025-2026. Important caveat: I could not check anything live in this run. The session's WebSearch budget was already used up (200 of 200), and the network proxy blocked every WebFetch domain I tried: wikipedia, k-eta.go.kr, korea.kr, mohw.go.kr, khidi.or.kr, koreaherald, koreatimes, bangkokpost, nationthailand and yna. The findings below therefore come from model knowledge, which runs to about mid-2026. Confidence is set conservatively. The URLs listed are official places to check each claim; they were not fetched this run. Every high_stakes item needs a live check before anyone relies on it.

findings.claim: Thai citizens can visit Korea without a visa for up to 90 days, but they still need a K-ETA approved before departure. As far as I know, Thailand has never been on Korea's temporary K-ETA exemption list.
findings.detail: The 90-day visa waiver comes from the Korea-Thailand visa waiver agreement and is well established. K-ETA became mandatory for visa-exempt nationals in 2021, with a fee of about KRW 10,000. The temporary exemption for 22 countries (US, Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, most of Western Europe, etc.) started in April 2023 and was extended to the end of 2025. It was reportedly extended again through 2026. As far as I know Thailand was never on that list, and Thai media repeatedly called this discriminatory. What this means for the clinic: every Thai patient has to get a K-ETA before flying. A K-ETA refusal or a denial at the airport cancels the procedure, so booking, deposit and refund policies have to account for that risk. I could not confirm Thailand's 2026 status live. Check it before publishing any 'how to come' content.
sources: https://www.k-eta.go.kr (official K-ETA portal - not fetched this run, verify exemption list)

findings.claim: Thai goodwill toward travel to Korea was damaged in 2023-2024 by entry denials and K-ETA refusals. The boycott hashtag #แบนเที่ยวเกาหลี trended, and Thai arrivals stayed well below the 2019 peak.
findings.detail: The root cause is Korea's large population of undocumented Thai workers. In Thailand they are called 'ผีน้อย' (phi noi, 'little ghosts'). Ministry of Justice figures I remember put them at roughly 140-160k, the largest undocumented group in Korea; this figure is unverified. Because of this, immigration officers at Incheon screen Thai tourists strictly, especially young women travelling alone. Viral stories of Thai tourists being questioned, held or sent home drove the boycott wave, which peaked around late 2023. In 2024 Thai arrivals reportedly fell year on year while most other ASEAN markets grew, so Thailand lost ground to markets like Vietnam and the Philippines. Pre-pandemic (2019), Korea received about 570k Thai visitors. I could not verify the exact 2023, 2024 or 2025 totals. For the clinic, this is the single biggest emotional barrier among Thai prospects: they fear being turned away at Incheon more than they worry about price.
sources: https://datalab.visitkorea.or.kr (KTO Tourism Data Lab, monthly arrivals by nationality - not fetched)

findings.claim: Korea's foreign-patient numbers roughly doubled in 2024, to about 1.17 million (reported at +93% from about 606k in 2023). Dermatology made up the majority, and aesthetic procedures drove the growth.
findings.detail: The Ministry of Health and KHIDI figures I remember, released in spring 2025: 1,170,467 foreign patients in 2024. Dermatology was the largest department at about 56-57%, followed by plastic surgery at about 11% and internal medicine at about 10%. The top nationalities were Japan, China, the US and Taiwan (Taiwan grew several-fold). Thailand was in the top group but with only a low single-digit share, very roughly 3-4%. My memory of Thailand's exact rank and count is weak, so I have not stated a number. The overall picture is strong: dermatology-led, Seoul-centred growth is exactly the segment a Shurink-only clinic sells into. The 2025 figures should have come out around April-May 2026, but I could not retrieve them.
sources: https://www.mohw.go.kr (MOHW press releases: '2024년 외국인환자 유치실적' - not fetched)
https://www.medicalkorea.or.kr (KHIDI Medical Korea portal, annual statistics by nationality and department - not fetched)

findings.claim: To recruit or advertise to foreign patients, a Korean clinic must first register with the Ministry of Health, through KHIDI, as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 under Medical Service Act Article 27-2. Paying unregistered brokers or agents to bring patients is illegal.
findings.detail: Article 27(3) of the Medical Service Act generally bans inducing or brokering patients. The exception for foreign-patient recruitment only applies to registered institutions and registered recruitment agencies (유치업자). Registration conditions include medical malpractice liability insurance, and registered institutions must report their foreign-patient numbers every year. For Thai marketing, this means: (1) register before any Thai-targeted campaign; (2) work only with registered agencies; (3) watch how commission-based Thai influencer or agent deals are structured. I am confident the articles exist. The detailed conditions, such as the insurance and specialist requirements, should be checked on law.go.kr.

findings.claim: The 10% VAT refund that foreign patients could claim on cosmetic dermatology and plastic surgery (in place since 2016) reportedly ended on 2025-12-31 and was not renewed in the 2025 tax revision.
findings.detail: I remember the 2025 tax revision (July 2025) as letting this special refund expire at the end of 2025, on the argument that the target of 1 million medical tourists had already been reached. If that is right, 2026 Thai patients effectively pay about 10% more than in 2025, and any Thai copy promising a 'tax refund' would be misleading. Confirm the current status before building price messaging.
sources: https://www.moef.go.kr (Ministry of Economy and Finance, 2025 세법개정안 - not fetched)
https://www.law.go.kr (조세특례제한법 의료관광 부가세 환급 특례 - not fetched)

findings.claim: Thai medical and beauty tourists mostly go to two Seoul clusters. Gangnam (Sinsa, Apgujeong, Cheongdam, around Gangnam Station) is seen as the 'serious' plastic surgery and dermatology district. Myeongdong is where tourists find walk-in dermatology chains near their hotels.
findings.detail: Thai first-time independent travellers mostly stay in Myeongdong, Hongdae or Dongdaemun. Gangnam is a 20-40 minute subway trip away (Line 2, or Line 4/3 with a transfer). In Thai the words 'กังนัม' and 'คลินิกเกาหลี' act as quality signals. Seoul accounts for the large majority of Korea's foreign patients. I remember a share above 80% for 2024 but could not verify it. If the clinic is in Gangnam, its Thai content should include step-by-step directions from Myeongdong and Hongdae hotels.
sources: https://www.medicalkorea.or.kr (regional distribution in annual report - not fetched)
https://datalab.visitkorea.or.kr (visited-area data by nationality - not fetched)

findings.claim: Bangkok to Seoul (Incheon) is about a 5.5-6 hour flight with many daily departures. Many are overnight red-eyes that leave Bangkok around midnight and land at Incheon early in the morning. Bangkok to Busan is about 5 hours.
findings.detail: Airlines on the Incheon route include Thai Airways, Korean Air, Asiana (being merged into Korean Air), Jeju Air, Jin Air, T'way and Air Premia. Thai AirAsia X flies from Don Mueang (DMK). Busan-Bangkok is served by LCCs such as Jeju Air and Air Busan, plus Korean Air, and there are some flights from Chiang Mai and Phuket. My sense is that off-peak LCC return fares are often in the low five figures in baht, roughly THB 8-15k, rising sharply in peak weeks. That is unverified, so check Skyscanner or Google Flights before quoting it. Operationally, the morning red-eye arrival and the last day of a trip are ideal slots for HIFU, which has little or no downtime.

findings.claim: Thai demand for Korea trips is seasonal. Peaks are Songkran and the Thai school summer break (April to mid-May), autumn leaves (mid-Oct to Nov), and the snow and year-end season (Dec to Feb). Snow and autumn foliage are especially strong draws for Thais.
findings.detail: Songkran holidays are April 13-15, often extended with bridge days. Thai schools break from about mid-March to mid-May, with a shorter break in October. The Dec 31-Jan 1 long weekend is a major travel window. Cherry blossoms in early April line up with Songkran. For ad timing, Thai travellers usually book flights 1-3 months ahead, so the clinic should start campaigns about 6-10 weeks before each peak: January-February for Songkran and April, August-September for foliage season, and October-November for snow and year-end.
sources: https://datalab.visitkorea.or.kr (monthly Thai arrivals to confirm seasonality - not fetched)

findings.claim: The typical Thai visitor to Korea is an independent traveller on a short trip of about 4-7 days, focused on Seoul, shopping, cafes, K-beauty and seasonal scenery. Medical or beauty treatment is usually an add-on to a leisure trip, not the sole purpose.
findings.detail: Because of this, a single-device, no-downtime procedure like Shurink or Ultraformer fits a leisure itinerary well. Swelling or bruising risk that could spoil holiday photos is a real concern, so the clinic should state recovery honestly. KTO's annual survey of foreign visitors (외래관광객조사) gives average stay and spending by nationality. I do not remember the Thai per-person spending figure reliably, so I have not given one.
sources: https://datalab.visitkorea.or.kr (외래관광객조사, spend and length of stay by nationality - not fetched)

findings.claim: Thai consumers already know 'Ultraformer III' (Thai: อัลตร้าฟอร์เมอร์) and can get it widely in Thai clinics. A trip to Korea is therefore not justified by device access or price alone.
findings.detail: Classys exports Shurink as Ultraformer III, and Thai clinic chains advertise it widely, often with per-line (shot-count) pricing. A Thai patient can easily compare prices at home. The Korean offer has to rest on things Thailand cannot copy: treatment by a Shurink-only specialist in Korea, the original manufacturer's genuine cartridges, Korean technique and design, and the experience of being treated in Korea's beauty capital during the trip. I have not given Thai price levels because I could not verify them.

findings.claim: The main messaging risks are colourism, the monarchy, religious imagery and the immigration or illegal-worker topic.
findings.detail: (1) Colourism: in 2016 a 'white = winner' ad for Seoul Secret whitening pills caused a major backlash in Thailand and was pulled. Avoid 'whiter' or 'fix your skin' framing and focus on lifting and firmness. (2) Monarchy: lèse-majesté (Thai Criminal Code Section 112) is enforced strictly; never use royal imagery, colours or references. (3) Buddha images: using them decoratively or commercially offends many Thais. (4) Never joke about or allude to 'ผีน้อย' or illegal workers, and do not imply that clinic paperwork guarantees entry. (5) Use native Thai copy with polite particles (ค่ะ/ครับ); machine-translated Thai signals low quality. (6) Thailand also has its own rules for health-facility advertising (e.g., the Sanatorium Act), which may restrict before/after photos and superlatives such as 'ดีที่สุด' (the best) in ads aimed at Thailand; that needs checking by the legal workstream.
sources: BBC / Thai press coverage, Jan 2016 'Seoul Secret whitening ad withdrawn' (URL not verified this run)

recommendations: Before any Thai-facing campaign, confirm or complete the clinic's registration as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 (Medical Service Act Art. 27-2), and work only with registered recruitment agencies. Structure Thai influencer or KOL deals so they are not commission-per-patient brokering unless the partner is a registered agency.

Build a Thai-language 'entry peace-of-mind kit' (ชุดเตรียมตัวเข้าเกาหลี), because entry-denial fear is the biggest barrier. It should include: a K-ETA how-to (apply well before booking non-refundable flights, fill in truthful details); an appointment confirmation letter on clinic letterhead in Thai and English with date, procedure and clinic address/phone for immigration; and a checklist (return ticket, hotel booking, proof of funds). Never state or imply that the clinic can guarantee entry.

Adjust booking policy to the K-ETA and entry risk: free rescheduling or a full deposit refund if a patient can document a K-ETA refusal or denial at entry. Advertising this policy is itself a trust signal.
Price in KRW with an approximate THB figure. Do not advertise a VAT or tax refund for 2026 until you have confirmed whether the cosmetic-procedure refund ended on 2025-12-31.
Run the ad calendar ahead of Thai travel peaks: January-February for Songkran and April; August-September for autumn foliage (Oct-Nov); October-November for snow and year-end (Dec-Feb).

Offer an 'arrival-day' or 'last-day' Shurink slot matched to overnight flight schedules (e.g., 10:00-13:00 on the day of an early-morning Incheon arrival), and say plainly that downtime is minimal, so holiday plans are not disrupted.

In Thai copy, lead with credibility that Thailand cannot copy: a Shurink-only specialist, the original Korean device and genuine cartridges, and Korean technique. Do not compete on price with Thai Ultraformer III clinics.

Provide a Thai-language map and step-by-step subway directions from Myeongdong and Hongdae hotels to the clinic. Use Thai-speaking coordination (a LINE Official Account is the default channel in Thailand).
Keep messaging clear of skin-whitening superiority, the monarchy, Buddha imagery and any immigration or illegal-worker jokes. Have a native Thai speaker review all creative.

Before finalising targets, pull the real numbers: KTO Data Lab monthly Thai arrivals for 2025 and 2026 year to date, and KHIDI/Medical Korea 2025 foreign-patient statistics for Thailand by department (dermatology share, total count, rank). All numbers in this brief were unverified in this run.
open_questions: As of September 2026, is Thailand on the K-ETA exemption list, or has Korea introduced any Thai-specific K-ETA easing (fast-track, group-tour exemption)? What is the current K-ETA refusal rate for Thai applicants?
How many Thai visitors came to Korea in 2025 and in 2026 so far? Has the post-boycott decline reversed? (Check KTO Data Lab.)
What are KHIDI's 2025 figures for Thai patients: total, rank among nationalities, and the dermatology vs plastic surgery split? Released around spring 2026 but not retrieved here.
Did the VAT refund on foreigners' cosmetic procedures definitely expire on 2025-12-31, or was it extended or replaced?
Is the clinic already registered as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관, and does it have malpractice insurance that covers foreign patients?
Where exactly is the clinic (Gangnam, Myeongdong, elsewhere)? That determines location messaging and which hotel districts to target.

Which Thai-side rules (Sanatorium Act advertising rules, Thai FDA rules on device naming and claims, Thai platform policies) apply to a Korean clinic running Thai-language ads on Meta, TikTok or LINE? This belongs to the legal workstream.
Current Bangkok-Seoul and Bangkok-Busan LCC fare levels in peak and off-peak weeks for 2026-2027, so the clinic can quote a realistic total trip cost.

checked.claim: Thai citizens can visit Korea without a visa for up to 90 days, but they still need a K-ETA approved before departure. As far as I know, Thailand has never been on Korea's temporary K-ETA exemption list.
evidence: VERIFICATION LIMIT: this run could not open any live source. The WebSearch quota was used up (200/200), and WebFetch to k-eta.go.kr, hikorea.go.kr, overseas.mofa.go.kr, koreaherald, bangkokpost, nationthailand, thaipbsworld, wikipedia and news.google was blocked by the egress proxy. This verdict rests on the reviewer's background knowledge up to mid-2026.

The core facts match my knowledge. Thai nationals get 90 days visa-free under the 1981 Korea-Thailand visa waiver agreement. K-ETA has been mandatory for visa-exempt nationals since Sept 2021. The fee is KRW 10,000 plus a small card-processing charge, about KRW 300. The 22-country/region temporary exemption started on 2023-04-01, originally ran to 2024-12-31, and was extended to 2025-12-31. Thailand was never on it.
I have a medium-confidence memory that the Ministry of Justice extended the 22-country exemption again to 2026-12-31. I did not verify it live, and I have no information that Thailand was added.
Nuance: saying 'Thai media repeatedly called this discriminatory' overstates it. The anger was mostly on Thai social media and Pantip, with the press reporting the backlash. Soften the wording.

Important for the clinic: a K-ETA refusal does not ban the traveller. They can still apply for a regular visa at the Korean Embassy in Bangkok, e.g. a short-term C-3 visa or, via a registered institution or agency, a C-3-3 medical-tourism visa. Booking policy should include this fallback, not just 'cancel'.

checked.claim: To recruit or advertise to foreign patients, a Korean clinic must first register with the Ministry of Health, through KHIDI, as a 외국인환자 유치의료기관 under Medical Service Act Article 27-2. Paying unregistered brokers or agents to bring patients is illegal.
checked.correction: The cited legal basis is outdated. The foreign-patient registration rules were moved out of the Medical Service Act when the '의료 해외진출 및 외국인환자 유치 지원에 관한 법률' (의료해외진출법) took effect in June 2016. Registration of a 외국인환자 유치의료기관, and of a 유치업자 (recruitment agency), is now under Article 6 of that Act, and Medical Service Act Art. 27-2 was deleted. The ban on inducing or brokering patients is still Medical Service Act Art. 27(3), and its proviso exempts recruitment of foreign patients by institutions and agencies registered under the 2016 Act. Registration conditions include malpractice liability insurance or mutual-aid coverage and at least one specialist in the relevant department. Registration is renewed periodically (I recall every 3 years) and results must be reported every year. Paying commissions to unregistered agents or brokers is illegal inducement. 'Must register before any advertising' is slightly overstated: registration is what makes recruitment lawful (agent commissions, patient discounts or incentives, brokered referrals). Plain informational foreign-language content is a grey area, so registering first is still the right advice. Also, 'foreign patient' under the Act excludes foreigners who live in Korea (registered residents, national health insurance holders), so marketing to Thais living in Korea is not covered by the exception. Confirm all article numbers and conditions on law.go.kr.
evidence: No live source opened (law.go.kr is egress-blocked). Background knowledge only.
Medium-high confidence that 의료해외진출법 (2016) Art. 6 is the current registration basis and that Medical Service Act Art. 27(3) proviso refers to it.

Low-medium confidence on the details: MOHW commission-rate caps for agencies (I recall roughly 15%, 20% and 30% by hospital tier), agency capital and guarantee-insurance requirements, and the renewal cycle. Verify each one.
Check (not fetched): https://www.law.go.kr/법령/의료해외진출및외국인환자유치지원에관한법률 ; https://www.law.go.kr/법령/의료법

checked.claim: Thai consumers already know 'Ultraformer III' (Thai: อัลตร้าฟอร์เมอร์) and can get it widely in Thai clinics. A trip to Korea is therefore not justified by device access or price alone.
evidence: No live source opened. Background knowledge only.

Classys exports Shurink as Ultraformer III, and the newer Ultraformer MPT corresponds to Shurink Universe in Korea. Both are widely advertised by Thai clinics with shot- or line-based pricing, which matches the claim.

Missing nuance: Thai consumers are wary of fake or refilled HIFU cartridges ('หัวปลอม' vs 'หัวแท้'), and genuine-cartridge verification is already a selling point in Thailand. 'Genuine cartridge, verified in Korea at the maker's home market' is therefore a credible differentiator, but it must be provable, e.g. by showing the cartridge being unsealed and its QR or authentication code.
Thai price levels are unverified. Do not publish comparisons without a dated price survey.

checked.claim: The main messaging risks are colourism, the monarchy, religious imagery and the immigration or illegal-worker topic.
evidence: No live source opened. Background knowledge only.

Seoul Secret (Jan 2016): a Thai-owned brand, despite the 'Seoul' name, ran a whitening-pill ad with actress Cris Horwang built on 'white makes you win'. It was pulled after a backlash and the company apologised. The fact that it was a Thai brand borrowing Korean-beauty cachet makes it even more relevant for a Korean clinic.

Precision on Thai ad law: the Sanatorium Act B.E. 2541 (1998) and Ministry of Public Health advertising rules, enforced by the Department of Health Service Support (สบส.), govern ads for health facilities licensed in Thailand. How they apply to a foreign clinic advertising into Thailand is unclear. Thai agents, influencers and platforms promoting the clinic could still be caught under Thai consumer-protection and health-advertising rules. Send this to the legal workstream and do not assume either way.
Add a risk: online Thai-Korean netizen flame wars, e.g. around entry denials and K-pop fandom spats. Avoid nationalistic comparisons ('Korea better than Thailand').
